events.event_narrative: In Hampton, the astronomical tide was 8.8 feet with a storm surge of 3.6 feet at high tide to reach a 12.4 foot storm tide. Flood stage in Hampton is 11.0 feet (MLLW). The Seavey Island tide gauge topped out at 11.6 feet (MLLW).  Widespread flooding occurred along the back bay area of Hampton with water inundation levels up to 18 inches deep.  Water entered the first floor of some residential buildings.  In addition, significant splash-over brought water onto Route 1A in Hampton Beach area due to large pounding surf.  In Rye, the water flooded Ocean Boulevard up to two feet deep.  Minor flooding was also reported in the Portsmouth area.

The astronomical tide in Portland of 9.6 feet combined with a storm surge of 3.1 feet at high tide to produce a 12.7 foot (MLLW) storm tide during the late morning hours. Flood stage in Portland is 12.0 feet (MLLW).  The tide remained above flood stage for a full three hours and 26 minutes at the Portland tide gage.  In Portland, the intersection of Somerset and Pearl streets flooded up to two feet deep near the Whole Foods grocery store.  Flooding was also reported along the Portland Pier with over a foot of inundation in the normal vulnerable low-lying areas.  The intense easterly winds and high storm tides led to closed roads due to large battering surf and water flooding inland tidal areas.  In Scarborough, route one was closed in both the north and south lanes due to flooding from the marsh.  Parking lots and roads were reported flooded in Cape Elizabeth.

Snow overspread the Mid-coast region of Maine just after midnight on March 3rd. Snow started off light before a localized heavier snowband developed towards the early morning hours across interior Lincoln County and Knox Counties.  Moderate to heavy snowfall fell in this band before it dissipated early in the morning. Snowfall amounts ranged from 6 to 8 inches.

Strong downslope winds on the lee-side of the Presidential Range of the White Mountains brought gusty southerly winds to the Lancaster/Littleton region of Coos County.  Numerous reports of downed trees and branches along with power lines were reported in this area.

After a very dry week with near record high temperatures on May 14th, a fire start was reported in Crawford Notch State Park.  The fire rapidly spread due to the dry fuels, slope alignment and favorable fire weather conditions.  Fire weather conditions quickly began to moderate by the evening of May 14th with rain falling on the fire.  The favorable conditions allowed fire fighters to get ahead of the fire with increased containment everyday.  Overall 107 acres were burned before full containment with mostly understory fuels burning.

A very brief but damaging tornado touched down in Chesterfield, NH |Monday night as a thunderstorm moved through the area. EF-0 damage |was initially observed on Mill Pond Rd. before the tornado became |stronger and caused significant tree damage supporting EF-1 |classification just north of Mill Pond. The tornado began to lift |shortly after the EF-1 damage with sporadic EF-0 damage before |quickly ending. The tornado damaged approximately 200 trees with a |few outbuildings being destroyed on the property. Tree damage included |uprooted hardwoods and softwoods, along with snapped trees.  Fortunately |no permanent residential structural damage was reported besides debris |clean up.

The long tracked severe thunderstorm that impacted the Moultonbourgh area strengthened once again as it traveled over Effingham, NH just after 3:30 PM. Widespread straight line wind damage began in western Effingham with a continuous area of wind damage concentrated along Town House Rd. Approximately 300 to 400 trees were either snapped or uprooted along this path of damage with sporadic tree damage throughout the town on other side roads.  Due to the observed almost |continues horizontal length of tree damage being near 4 miles, this outflow wind damage is characterized as a macroburst. A few buildings were damaged due to trees falling on roofs, but no injuries were reported from this event.

A long tracked severe thunderstorm and associated microburst reached the Moultonbourgh Neck area of Lake Winnipesaukee just after 3pm. The damaging winds downed over 200 trees on the western shore of the lake, with uprooted and snapped trees. The outflow winds then fanned across Moultonbourgh Bay, damaging trees on remote islands and the eastern shore of the lake where another area of concentrated damage occurred along the immediate shoreline.  Another 50 or so trees fell in this |area.  Overall 5 buildings were damaged but no injuries were reported. The storm continued to move eastward with continued sporadic damage though Ossipee before it reached Effingham, NH.

A severe thunderstorm and associated microburst reached the western shore of Sebago Lake just after 4pm.  The damaging winds downed 80 to 100 trees...some uprooted and others snapped.  Most of the trees were softwoods while a few were hardwoods. About fifteen structures were damaged along with ten vehicles.  One fatality occurred when a tree fell on an occupied vehicle.  The most significant damage occurred within a one mile path width and within a quarter mile of the western shore of Sebago Lake. Sporadic damage occurred beyond this.  This storm would continue to produce|additional wind damage as it moved east of Sebago Lake later in the afternoon.

On the August 2nd drought monitor, York County was 66% in severe drought and 34% in moderate drought. By the end of the month, 2% of the county was in severe drought, 70% in moderate drought, and 27% abnormally dry. The improved designations were the result of scattered heavy rainfall, notably on the 22nd where areas received up to 6 inches. The highest accumulated rainfall for the month fell in Hollis with 9.12 inches for the month. |The state of Maine activated its Drought Task Force in July 2022. Several towns instituted voluntary water restrictions. Hydro operators balanced needs of lake levels, hydroelectric power generation needs, and the discharges to maintain stream flow needs downstream. Most of the reported water quantity issues were from southern and coastal areas. Farmers without irrigation experienced stressed vegetation from a lack of rain and above normal temperatures in July. First-cut hay crop was near normal, but subsequent hay growth was slowed. Most streamflow stations in central and southern rivers with 30+ years of record were between the 10th-25th percentiles compared to normal.

A hiker planned to summit Mount Lafayette in the White Mountains on November 19-20th.  The hiker didn't return to the trailhead as planned on Sunday and because of the harsh winter conditions a search party was immediately initiated that evening.  Because of the harsh winter conditions bringing low visibility, blowing snow and cold wind chills the Search and Recovery mission was hampered.  The search party spent the next two days looking for the hiker until her body was found on Wednesday in the upper elevations of Mount Lafayette.  Cause of death was recorded as exposure to the elements.

The Ellis River reached flood stage on the evening of the 14th cresting at 17.51 feet in the evening. The covered bridge in Andover was flooded along with the adjacent road. Storm total rainfall  was measured at 4.53 inches in Andover.

The Swift River came out of banks midday on the 14th and crested at 9.8 feet, almost three feet above flood stage.  The closure of Route 17 in Byron near the intersection of Byron Village Road resulted in significant impact to access in and out of the region. The river flooded as a result of heavy rainfall measured 4.53 inches in Andover in a nearby watershed, with comparable rainfall having fallen over the Swift basin.

A strong storm system brought widespread moderate to heavy rain with added upslope enhancement in the White Mountains. The storm total water in the Upper Saco watershed was between 3 to 4 inches of rainfall. Some nearby rainfall reports include 4.41 in Jackson, 3.82 in Intervale, and 3.57 in Brookfield. The Saco River at Conway came out of banks exceeding flood stage 9.0 feet during the early afternoon of the 14th, and crested at 10.22 feet.  Floodwaters surrounded properties across Transvale Acres in Conway. Flood waters were 1 to 2 feet deep in sections of east bank camping areas.

A second during the morning to midday period featured wind gusts of 60 to 65 mph. The final round of strong wind gusts occurred with a band of thunderstorms as they moved across southern New Hampshire in the early evening.

Snow began during the afternoon on the 25th as a band of light precipitation well ahead of the main precipitation shield. The steady snowfall moved into central New Hampshire during the evening hours on the 25th. Moderate snow continued until just after midnight, when mid level warming allowed sleet and freezing rain to take over as the dominant precipitation types. Eventually precipitation changed over to rain before coming to an end on the morning of the 26th. The existing and new snowfall absorbed much of the sleet, freezing rain, and rain that fell. Snowfall totals suffered from significant compaction by the time of most reports in the morning, but generally ranged from 5 to 7 inches.

Water inundated route 1A along North Beach at least 3.5 feet deep. Debris such as rocks and sand was strewn over Ocean Boulevard from strong wave action. Sections of Route 100 were closed as well as Route 1 on the Hampton and Hampton Falls city line as the marsh overflowed. Many water rescues were required as driver attempted to cross the flood waters or from residents trapped in their flooded homes. The morning of December 23rd had perfect alignment of a very high astronomical tide, peak storm surge of 2+ feet and large battering nearshore waves of 15 to 20 feet all coinciding at high tide.  The astronomical tide in Portland was 11.3 feet MLLW at 10:16 am, already close to the established 12 foot MLLW minor flood level. The intense onshore winds produced a storm surge of 2.41 feet in Portland Harbor.  The resulting storm tide topped out at 13.72 feet MLLW, it���s fourth highest water level in modern history for the Forest City (records 1912-present). The tide remained above flood stage for 195 minutes (945 am - 100 pm). A temporary new tide gauge installed by the Gulf of Maine Research Institute (GMRI) in Portland reached 13.78 feet MLLW. Snowfall had a high snow to liquid ratio, and fell at an inch per hour at times. Light snow continued into the evening on the 23rd. The astronomical tide in Portland was 11.3 feet MLLW at 10:16 am, already close to the established 12 foot MLLW minor flood level. The intense onshore winds produced a storm surge of 2.41 feet in Portland Harbor.  The resulting storm tide topped out at 13.72 feet MLLW, it���s fourth highest water level in modern history for the Forest City (records 1912-present). The tide remained above flood stage for 195 minutes (945 am - 100 pm). A temporary new tide gauge installed by the Gulf of Maine Research Institute (GMRI) in Portland Back Cove reached 13.78 feet MLLW.  Across the southern tip of Maine at the relatively new Seavey Island gauge, the tide reached 12.41 feet MLLW at 1054 am with a storm surge of 2.50 feet.||Significant to major coastal flooding occurred across most vulnerable locations in Cumberland County.  Significant flooding occurred along the city wharfs and side streets in Portland with inundation of up to 2 feet that included Amethyst Park, the Portland Pier, the Harbor Fish Market, Union Wharf, Widgery Wharf as well as the Custom House Wharf. Portions of Marginal Way also flooded but inundation levels were slightly less.  Flooding also occurred in the Back Cove area to include the Bayside Trail, Sewage Plant Rd. and parts of Commercial Street.  South Portland had flooding along Willard Beach and Bug Light State Park.  The historic seawall of Fort Preble was damaged due to large battering waves.  The iconic Portland Head Light was damaged as large battering waves crashed into the building which blew out windows and flooded the building in Cape Elizabeth.  Additional wave damage to roads with tons of rock debris on roads that had to plowed in Cape Elizabeth. Further south, Scarborough experienced flooding on Black Point Rd. Haggis Parkway, Payne Road and sections of Route 1.

Ice flows from Gorham were transported downstream to Rumford on December 23rd when rain and snowmelt raised river levels. The ice jammed at the Rumford dam, causing fast rising water during the early morning hours of December 24. All three roads into Rumford from the west were flooded. Route 232 and Route 2 were severely flooded with water 1 to 5 feet deep. Flood waters entered around a dozen properties, including the first floor of at least 5 structures. Multiple cold water rescues were conducted for motorists surprised by the flooded roads at night. No fatalities or injuries were reported.

Moderate rainfall coincided with a very high astronomical tide and storm surge, resulting in overtopped storm drains and flooding in low-lying urban areas.  Several portside business and parking lots were inundated. The flooding was a combination of freshwater runoff and high tide storm surge.
A squall line embedded in the stronger synoptic wind storm mixed down damaging winds to the surface.  A 71 mph wind gust was reported at Manchester Airport when the line pushed through.
Convective wind gusts associated with a thunderstorm squall line downed a tree on a moving car in Durham New Hampshire.
Convective wind gusts associated with a squall line downed a tree onto a vehicle in Dover.
Convective winds gusts associated with a squall line downed multiple trees that closed a road in Brentwood.

Snow accumulation was highly dependent on elevation, with the lowest totals around I-93 in the Pemigewasset Valley. Snowfall totals ranged from 3 to 4 inches in the valley, to 12 inches in the higher terrain.

Rain changed to snow in the Lakes Region during the morning on the 14th. Snowfall quickly became moderate to heavy at times, especially south and east of Lake Winnipesaukee. In the lowest elevations, where winds were downsloping off the Ossipees, snow totals were around 2 to 3 inches. In the higher terrain of southeast Belknap County snow totals were as high as 15 inches.

Rain changed to snow in the Lakes Region during the early morning on the 14th. Snowfall quickly became moderate to heavy at times, especially near the Ossipees. Wwhere winds were downsloping off the mountains snow totals were around 4 inches. In the higher terrain southeast of Lake Winnipesaukee snow totals were as high as 19 inches.

Rain changed to snow in the Merrimack Valley during the early morning on the 14th. Snowfall quickly became moderate to heavy at times, especially in the higher terrain. In the lowest elevations around I-93 snowfall totals were around 5 or 6 inches. In the higher terrain around Mount Sunapee snow totals were as high as 24 inches. Power outages were widespread where snowfall totals exceeded 10 inches.

Rain changed to snow in the Lakes Region during the early morning on the 14th. Snowfall quickly became moderate to heavy at times, especially in the higher terrain. Rain changed to snow in the Merrimack Valley during the early morning on the 14th. Snowfall quickly became moderate to heavy at times, especially farther from the coast. Rain changed to snow at the Seacoast during the morning on the 14th. Snowfall became moderate to heavy at times during the afternoon, where snowfall rates and lower sun angle helped snow accumulate. Snowfall totals ranged from 6 to 10 inches.

River Road washed out by excessive runoff from 5.0 to 5.5 inches of rainfall on the morning of May 1. Road impassable for over a month.
A water rescue was needed around Route 17 in North Jay/Wilton town line for a car washed off the road.
Flash floods caused a washout on Greenwoods Road after 3.5 to 4.5 inches of rainfall fell on the morning of May 1.

Heavy rainfall between 3 and 4 inches fell over Dixfield on the morning of May 1. The heavy rain over saturated ground caused a washout on Averill Hill Road. Severy Hill and Valley Road were closed due to flooding.  Route 164 and Coolidge Road had multiple washouts along the edge of the road. A significant washout occurred on Valley Brook Road.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 and 4.5 inches on already saturated ground resulted in a washout on Maine Route 108.
Heavy rainfall of 3.5 to 4.5 inches on the morning of May 1 resulted in a washout on South Rumford Road.
Heavy rainfall caused the Swift River to rapidly rise and washout on Roxbury Notch Road.
Washout on Mount Micha Road after approximately 4 inches of rain fell on already saturated ground on the morning of May 1.
Multiple washouts between Gore Road and Hidden Lake Road on the morning of May 1 after 3.5 to 4.5 inches of rain fell over already saturated ground.
Washout occurred on Rabbit Valley Road in Otisfield after 3.5 to 4.5 inches of rain fell on saturated ground early in the morning of May 1.
Heavy rainfall estimated between 3.5 to 4.5 inches on the morning of May 1 resulted in a washout on Webbs Mills Road.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 to 4.5 inches fell over saturated ground on the morning of May 1. The runoff caused a washout on Waterford Road.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 to 4.5 inches fell over already saturated ground on the morning of May 1. The resultant flash flood washed out a portion of Route 160.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 to 4.5 inches over already saturated ground resulted in a washout on Route 117 in Denmark.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 to 4.5 inches fell over already saturated ground resulting in a 4 foot sinkhole on Smith Road.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 to 4.5 inches caused a washout on Route 5 in Lovell.
Heavy rainfall between 3.5 to 4.5 inches caused flooding on Stow Road or Maine Route 113 resulting in a water rescue.
Flooding on North Road in Gilead resulted in a water rescue to a motorist.
Heavy rain resulted in a washout on Gibson Road in West Bethel.
Heavy rainfall resulted in excessive runoff and a rapid rise in the Sunday River. A vehicle was stuck in flood waters and necessitated a water rescue on Sunday River Road.
Heavy rain caused a washout on Maine Route 156 in Weld.

Heavy rainfall measured between 4 to 5.5 inches fell across Androscoggin County. Small streams rapidly responded with flooding in several communities including Livermore, Turner, Auburn, Leeds, and Wales. The hardest hit area was Wales where numerous road closures including Route 132 which significantly disrupted travel in and out of the area. A washout on Turkey Lane in Livermore led to basement flooding of a nearby property.

The Sheepscot River came out of banks and flooded portions of High Tide Road or Route 194 just south of Hollywood Boulevard. Floodwaters were up to the foundations of a few homes. The river crested at 8.56 feet around 6 PM on the evening of May 1. Floodwaters damaged Route 194.
Heavy rain resulted in a small pond overtopping and flooding Route 218 in south of Alna with 2 to 3 feet of water. The pond drains into Dyer River, a small tributary of the Sheepscot River.

Heay rainfall resulted in numerous road closures and washouts across Brownfield including Sam Brown Hill Road, Hampshire Road, Merrill Corner Road and Dugway Road. There were numerous washouts on Old County Road.

Heavy rain caused the Swift River to come out of banks and flood portions of Byron and Roxbury. The river came out of banks during the early morning hours which caused the closure of Maine Route 17, that resulted in significant disruption to travel in and out of the area. The river crested at 10.8 feet by early afternoon, which is 3.8 feet above flood stage.

Heavy rainfall caused the Kennebec River to overflow its banks and cause flooding in Skowhegan and Winslow. Flooding was observed on the southbound lane of Route 2 in Skowhegan near Malbons Mills Road. Campground flooding was up to 2 feet deep on the east side of town. Fort Halifax Park in Winslow flooded. The river peak flow was measured around 76k cfs on May 2.

The Carrabassett River rose 7 feet above flood stage on May 1 after 3 to 4 inches of rain fell over the watershed. The river crested at 22.08 feet in the early afternoon, reaching the 2nd highest flow since the flood of April 1987.  Impacts included flooding of Route 27 north of Kingfield, Route 16 and Route 146 in New Portland. Widespread low lying flooding including impacts to agricultural fields were observed in North Anson.

The headwaters of the Sandy River came out of banks and flooded the basements and garages of homes in Phillips and closed Route 142 and 149. Additional roads that flooded were Bray Hill Road, East Madrid Road, Weld Road, Bridge Street, Salem Road near Auger Drive, #6 road. The USGS river gage at Madrid indicated the river crested at 10.64 feet, which was just below the highest peak on record for this short period of record gauge. In Madrid Township River Road flooded.

Floodwaters from the Sandy River combined with local runoff from the Beaver Brook in Farmington to cause significant flooding along Main Street by the Hippach Field as well as Front Street. Floodwaters inundated Abbott Park with water several feet deep. Businesses on Main Street had floodwaters of a few inches deep within their first floors. The USGS river gage in Madrid crested at a stage of 10.6 feet and the Mercer gage crested at 14.62 feet, both 2 to 4 feet above flood stage. The high flows on the Sandy River resulted in backwater along the Temple Stream which flooded a business off Route 2 & 4 in Farmington.

Flooding along the Sandy River between Phillips and Strong caused numerous road closures including parts of Route 4 and River Road. Hardest hit was in Avon where backwater along a brook paralleling the Avon Valley Road flooded a home.

Multiple washouts on College Road train tracks flooding and again near the Stetson Brook crossing. Multiple washouts on Lane Road from an un-named stream that flows into Stetson Brook. Road washouts on both South and North Mountain Roads. Road washed away on Morse Cemetary Road after an un-named stream overwhelmed a culvert. Damage to bridge on South Mountain Road.
Moose Hill Pond overtopped and caused excessive flows on Redwater Brook. This resulted in flooding of the water treatment plant and significant damages.
Multiple washouts on Carsley Road in Harrison.

The Carrabassett River rose 7 feet above flood stage on May 1 after 3 to 4 inches of rain fell over the watershed. The river crested at 22.08 feet in the early afternoon, reaching the 2nd highest flow since the flood of April 1987. Floodwaters washout Island Road cutting off residential properties.

Flash flooding caused washouts on multiple roads in the town of Industry. Those roads include Greenwood Brook Road, Shaw Hill Road, New Sharon Road, Baily Road with multiple washouts, and Federal Row.
Town of Hartford sustained a washout between Route 219 and 140 and damage to two bridges.
Flooding of the Darnit Brook damaged Rosenburg and Decoster Roads in Sumner. Decoster Road sustained multiple washouts near the brook crossing and two of five culvers.
Flash flooding caused numerous shoulder washouts on roads across West Paris. The hardest hit road was along Ellingwood Road near Ryerson Hill Road where a complete washout occurred.
Flash flooding caused washouts on numerous roads in Woodstock including Redding Road, Concord Road, Pond Road, and Swinton Road.
Bridge washout on Fern Road in Lovell from the Kezar River.
Rounds of heavy rainfall resulted in flooding of small streams in Washington. The Little Medomack Brook washout out part of Calderwood Road and Davis Stream flooded Varner road.
Significant damage to Spring Run Hill Road in Edgecomb after an un-named tributary to the Deer Meadow Brook flooded 325 feet of roadway. Multiple Culverts and 175 feet of roadway washed out.

Rainfall measured between 3.5 to 5.15 inches fell across Cumberland County between April 30 and May 1. This rainfall caused flooding of numerous low lying roads and multiple road closures. The Royal River flooded a portion of Route 211 in North Gloucester causing its closure for 2 days.
A portion of Main Street flooded.
Route 41 flooded in Farmington.
Interval Road flooded in Temple.
Manor Road flooded in Rangeley.
Bray Bill Road flooded in Wilton/Salem.
Flooding on Route 27 and 234 in New Vineyard.
Norton Hill Road flooded and closed.
West Kingfield Road closed after the West Branch of the Carrabasset River flooded.
Route 27 flooded in Mount Vernon near Belgrade Lakes.
A combinate of high lake levels on Great Pond and heavy rainfall caused flooding on Route 225 in Rome.

Widespread and numerous flooded roads across Knox County. Coastal flooding was concurrent with the heavy rainfall and increased the impacts. Roads that were flooded include Route 1 in Camden, Route 105 in Hope and Washington, Route 126 in Jefferson, and Route 131 near Campground Road in Appleton.
Greenwood Road impassable due to flooding.
Hardscrabble Road closed due to flooding.
West Branch of the Nezinscot River flooded Redding Road Bridge.
Runoff from Jim Hill in Norway flooded and resulted in the closure of Route 118.
Runoff from Hemingway Ridge caused the Swift Cambridge River to flood and close the major access Route 26, leading to significant disruption to travel in and out of the region.
Heavy rain caused excessive runoff from the Camden Hills. This resulted in flooding on Route 52 in Hope and Route 220 in Montville.
Heavy rain caused flooding across York County including Route 11 in Limerick and Route 202 in Lebanon. County rain gage reports range rom 3.5 to 4.7 inches in Limington.

The Androscoggin River reached flood stage during the morning of May 1. Flood waters out of Gorham flooded areas from Gilead, to extensive flooding in Bethel and Rumford. Flooding started at North Road in Gilead, followed by Route 26 in Bethel between Cross Street and Intervale Road. In Rumford, South Rumford Road flooded.  Low spots flood along the Swift and Androscoggin Rivers in Mexico and Rumford flooded including parks and boat launches. The USGS river gage in Rumford crested at 15.76 feet, less than a foot above flood stage.

The Kennebec River came out of banks and on May 1 and caused significant flooding to several businesses between Augusta and Gardiner. The discharge measured at the USGS river gage in Sydney, just upstream of Augusta, had a 10 year peak flow of 113,000 cfs, which is tied as the third highest streamflow with June 1, 1984 and exceeded only by the flood of 1987 and 1936.  The river crested at 20.3 feet in Augusta and 16.8 feet in Hallowell, just shy of the 18 foot stage for major flood level. The flooding was the result of a basin average of 4.5 inches, most of which ran off from nearly saturated ground conditions. ||The most significant impacts occurred in Gardiner along the confluence of the Cobbosseecontee Stream and the Kennebec River, both of which were running at flood levels.  The overflow resulted in flooding of parking lots and basements between Water Street and Arcade Street and businesses south of Bridge Street and Main Avenue. Flood waters were reported of 2 to 3 feet deep in parking lots.  Flooding was prevalent along Front Street in Augusta and Hallowell where basement flooding occurred along several businesses and apartment complexes, including a US Postal Service building. Over a dozen vehicles flooded after waters submerged parking lots. The impacts were most notable on the west bank of the Kennebec River with minimal impacts on the east bank.

Heavy rain estimated around 3.5 inches cause an un-named small stream to the Fish Brook to overwhelm a culvert on Green Road in Fairfield. The resulting flood washed out a 10 foot section of the road.
Locally heavy rain caused New Hampshire Route 113 to close due to flooding in multiple areas between Tamworth and Madison. Route 153 was closed due to flooding in Eaton.
Locally heavy rain caused Route 16B flooding at the intersection of Route 16 in Center Ossipee.

The Saco River came out of banks on May 1st that caused significant flooding to several camps and campgrounds between Conway and Bartlett.  The flooding significantly impacted travel in and out of the area due to closed roads. Flooding started on the upper portion of the West Side Road with minor property inundation. The floodwater moved downstream causing significant damage to area campgrounds in North Conway and backwater on the Ellis River.  In North Conway a section of West Side Road flooded, cutting off access to several homes. River Road flooded on the west bank of the Saco River flooding agricultural lands.  Floodwaters inundated first floors of properties in Transvale Acres.  Moat Brook Road flooded cutting off seasonal camps. Widespread agricultural flooding occurred between Conway and Fryberg.  The river levels were at the bridge deck of the Saco River Covered Bridge in Conway.  The USGS river gage in Conway crested at a 13.6 feet, exceeding the 9 foot flood stage by 4.6 feet.

Rainfall between 0.5 and 1.25 inches fell over still frozen soils in portions of the White Mountains during the morning of May 1. The excessive runoff resulted in significant and multiple washouts on the Kancamangus Highway in Lincoln, which lies between the steep slopes of mountains peaking over 3,000 feet.

A thunderstorm with torrential rain brought flash flooding to urban areas in southern Nashua. Unofficial weather stations in the area reported instantaneous rainfall rates between 3 and 4 inches per hour, with rainfall totals between 1.75 and 2.25 inches. The rapid runoff overflowed storm water drainage systems which had limited capacity from earlier rainfall. Water up to 2 feet deep was reported on Daniel Webster Highway.

A cluster of thunderstorms moved over Salem between 3 and 430 pm. An unofficial weather station recorded rainfall up to 4.25 inches in the area with instantaneous rates peaking around 4 inches per hour. The rapid runoff over this urban area resulted in a foot of water on Route 28, disrupting the evening commuter traffic.

A hard freeze impacted the region shortly after midnight on May 18th with widespread sub-freezing temperatures.  Temperatures ranged from freezing to the mid-20s.  Lewiston airport reported a low of 26 degrees.  The temperatures were some of the coldest this late in spring in over the past 30 years based on official records.  The hard freeze impacted blooming fruit trees and berries the most.  The hardest hit orchards were those at lower elevations in valleys with less impacts at orchards located at slightly higher elevations on hills.  There were reports of flower mortality rate as high as 90% in some areas.  In addition, leaf kill was prevalent with some oak species due to these tree species being more vulnerable to freezing.

Rainfall between 0.5 and 1.25 inches fell over still frozen soils in portions of the White Mountains during the morning of May 1. The excessive runoff resulted in significant and multiple washouts on the Mount Washington Auto-road in the White Mountains.

A National Weather Service storm survey found that a tornado touched down near Base Hill Road in North Swanzey in Cheshire County and briefly lifted before touching down again near Route 101 near the Keene/Marlboro line. A few spotters viewed a rotating wall cloud and funnel as it moved near this location.  EF-1 damage was found in Marlboro due to damage to soft and hardwood trees along with some trees falling into parked vehicles. The tornado then intermittently skipped eastward nearly right along Route 101 downing hundreds of trees along the way but no structures were damaged, before arriving in Dublin.  It is there where trees fell on cars and buildings, ripped siding and shingles off of structures, broke windows, and knocked down several hundreds of large healthy trees. The tornado then lifted for good before reaching the intersection of Route 101 and Monument Road in Dublin.  Overall an estimated amount of around 1000 trees were uprooted or snapped.  5 buildings were partial damages, along with damage to small out buildings, some boats and a few parked vehicles.

Grantham Mountain Road in Meriden, N.H. nearing the intersection with Route 120 was washed out in the afternoon of the 17th. The flood washed out over 300 feet of road material, including asphalt, with crevices of as much as 10-feet deep in some places. Radar estimated about 3 inches of rain fell between 2:30 p.m. and 4:30 p.m. The rain flooded Bloods Brook, which runs parallel to Grantham Mountain Road before entering a large culvert, approximately 4 feet in diameter, that passes underneath the road. The culvert was overwhelmed and the road subsequently damaged.
NH Route 11 had 2 to 3 feet of water over the road.

In Newport, stormwater flooded the drainage system on Sand Hill Road, washing away about 150 feet of the dirt road. The washout affected a handful of homeowners who lived on the dead-end portion of the road. A half-dozen other roads, including Fletcher Road and a portion of Maple Street, also were also washed away.

Heavy rainfall estimated by radar between 2 and 3 inches fell during the early afternoon of June 17.  In Croydon several roads were flooding including Brighton Road, Winter Road and Croydon Brook Road. Croydon Brook Road sustained washouts.
Road shoulder washout on Route 4 in Enfield.

Heavy downpours fell over the hilly terrain around Alexandria New Hampshire during the overnight hours of the 26th. The heaviest rain fell around Mt. Cardigan and surrounding hills with radar estimates between 3 and 5 inches. Heavy rainfall caused flooding of several small streams including Bailey, Clark, Brock, Patten, and Bog Brooks. Much of the flood damage was from overflow of the Patten and Bog Brooks. Significant washouts and closures occurred on Bailey Road, Burns Hill Road, Plummer Hill Road, Thissel Road, Bog Road, King Road, and Town Pound Road. In Alexandria shelters were open to house displaced residents as access was cut off for hundreds of residents.

The Newfound River came out of its banks after 4 to 6 inches of rainfall in the early morning hours of the 26th. Pleasant Street in Bristol sustained a washout, with 4 feet of sand and gravel piled into intersection of Lake Street by floodwaters. Numerous roads washed out elsewhere in the community with culverts exposed and pavement collapsed, including Plummer Hill, Matthews Rd, Burns Hill, Foster Pond, and King Rd.

Considerable flash flooding occurred in Andover on the morning of the 26th after 3 and 6 inches of rain fell along the south facing slopes of the Wyman Mountain. Abbott Brook was redirected and severely impacted Wyman Hill Road and personal property along it. At one stretch along Wyman Hill Rd, Abbott Brook was diverted and is running directly down the middle of the road. More than a dozen residents were impacted, leaving people without road access. The main bridge at Wyman Hill Rd and Cross Rd was washed out. There was also one water rescue in Andover as a vehicle got stuck in the flood waters. The runoff caused the Ellis River to climb above flood stage cresting at 17.29 feet.||Additional roads in Andover that sustained washouts were East B Hill Road and South Arm Road. The major thruway of Route 120 was closed from Route 5 to Roxbury Pond Road due to flooding out of the Ellis River.

Heavy rainfall between 3 and 4 inches fell across the headwaters of the Swift River during the early morning hours of the 26th. The resultant runoff caused the river to rise above flood stage (7Ft) and crest at 8.32 feet around 945 AM based on data from the USGS river gage in Roxbury. State Route 17 is closed in Roxbury due to flooding from Frye Crossover Road to Black Ridge Road.

Multiple rounds of moderate to heavy rainfall overwhelmed Manchester storm drainage systems resulting in urban flooding. Flooding was reported on Green Street and Beech Street. Water up to car hoods. A report of water up to people���s knees on the intersection of Lake Avenue and Pine Street.
Flooding on NH Route 123 in Ipswich. Widespread flooding surrounding numerous businesses near Camden Court and Davis Village Road.

Heavy rain estimated between 3.5 to 5.5 inches fell between 7 and 930 pm across West Chesterfield, with rainfall rates measured over 3 inches per hour. This torrential rainfall resulted in flooding across sections of Main Street, Brook Street, Streeter Hill Road, and Gulf Road. Washouts were reported on Gulf Road.
Pond Brook surged out of banks and onto Pond Brook Drive near Chamberlain Way.

Repeated rounds of rainfall between the 26th and 28th saturated the ground, and by the afternoon of the 28th the runoff was rapid and produced flash flooding. Heavy rainfall caused flooding on NH-109, eroded ditches along the side of the road, undermining the edge of the roadway.  There was a partial washout of Bald Peak Dr in the area of NH-109.

Nearly 6 inches of rain fell near Rockwood and Brassua Lake in northern Somerset County. Multiple washouts on Route 6 between Brassua and Jackman caused significant disruption to travel in the region.

Heavy rain fell across Enchanted Pond just south of Jackman between 5 and 7 PM, bringing a radar estimate of 4 inches, most of which fell between 530 and 6 PM. This torrential rainfall caused a small retention pond in the hills above the lake to collapse. The resultant debris flow included uprooted trees and boulders, along with high flowing water around 3 feet deep. A campground located below the hill sustained significant damage.
Flooding with severe shoulder washouts on Route 201 near Parlin Pond.

Flooding in Rockwood causing significant disruptions to travel in and out of the region. Most of the downtown village was impacted. Roads flooded include Misery Gorge and Marston, Cedar, and Village Roads.

Flooding on Route 15 west of Rockwood after heavy rain fell during the afternoon of June 29. The radar estimated rainfall amounts of 3 to 5 inches, most of which fell in an hour between 3 and 4 pm. Multiple significant washouts occurred.

Washout on Gale Road near Fowler Road intersection in Alexandria, when the Fowler River left its banks. Flooding on Berea Road in Hebron with flood damage to outbuildings.
Washout on Gerrish Road in Salisbury from overflow of the Allen Brook.
Flooding on Tin Mile Road with road damage in Jackson.
Significant washout on Stevens Rd, culverts overflowed and exposed, approximately 2000 ft of pavement washout.

A concentrated area of 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across southern Franklin County during the afternoon of June 29th into the early evening hours. Between 400 pm and 700 pm, a stalled thunderstorm brought 2 to 3 inch per hour rainfall rates which peaked between 430 pm and 600 pm where most of the rain fell. These rains fell across previously saturated soils and hilly terrain. The heaviest rain fell in Jay.  An additional 17 roads in surrounding communities of Wilton, Farmington, and Chesterville sustained partially wash-outs or road closures from flooding.  In nearby Wilton, ME-156 at Soules Hill Road and Whittier Roads sustained washouts.

A concentrated area of 3 to 6 inches of rain fell across southern Franklin County during the afternoon of June 29th into the early evening hours. Between 400 pm and 700 pm, a stalled thunderstorm brought 2 to 3 inch per hour rainfall rates which peaked between 430 pm and 600 pm where most of the rain fell. These rains fell across previously saturated soils and hilly terrain. Flooding developed quickly and the hardest hit community of Jay had considerable damage. More than a dozen roads sustained significant washouts and were closed to traffic. Several major roads including Routes 4, 140, and 133 in Jay were damaged. A bridge was washed out on Macomber Hill Road and another in Woodman Hill Road in North Jay. Several homes were cut off for an extended period of time due to complete washouts. The majority of the damage was to infrastructure from roads to public sewer systems, however some property damage was incurred to driveways, yards, and basements. The following roads in Jay were reported flooded; Route 133 between Farmington and East Jay Road, Route 156 between Davis Road and Soules Hill Road, Franklin Road between Hyde and Beedy Roads, Old Jay Hill Road, Intervale Road, Macomber Road near Lomie Rivers Road, Murphy���s Lane washout, Davenport Hill Road major washouts, Canton Mountain Road major washouts, Look Brook Circle major washouts, 900 Block of East Jay Road, and Keep Road.

Flash flooding occurred in Bryon on the morning of the 26th after 3 and 5 inches of rain fell along the south facing slopes of the Wyman Mountain. Garland Pond Road, Dingle Hill Road, #6 Road to Weld, Buckfield Hill Road, Lohnes Farm Road and Route 17 all sustained damage. Garland Pond Road, Dingle HIll Road and #6 Roads were not passable for more than 24 hours.
Heavy rainfall estimated around 2 inches caused Cobbetts Pond Road to suffer a shoulder washout. Flooding was partially caused by an undersized culvert.

Falls Brook came out of banks and flooded Hale Hill Road on the evening of July 3rd. A small thunderstorm intensified over East Swanzey with high rainfall rates peaking around 3 inches per hour. The radar estimated 2 to 3 inches of storm total precipitation over the headwaters of Falls Brook in the Little Monadnock Mountains.

A thunderstorm brought heavy rain to the Monadnock Mountain region causing flash flooding in Troy.  Rainfall rates peaked around 3 inches per hour and estimated between 1 to 3 inches fell in the Troy area. Russell Rd washed out from hillside runoff.	Monadnock Street at Nelson Street closed due to flooding.

A thunderstorm brought heavy rain to the Monadnock Mountain region causing flash flooding between Troy and Jaffrey.  Rainfall rates peaked around 3 inches per hour and estimated between 1 to 3 inches fell across the area. State Route NH-124 near Bollard Road in Jaffrey had shoulder damage due to wash-outs from flooding.

A storm brought torrential rainfall south of Swanzey on the evening of the 3rd. Swanzey Lake Road washed out near Dunn Hill Road. Radar estimated rainfall between 1 to 3 inches fell within an hour shortly before midnight.

Torrential rainfall with rates over 3 inches per hour fell across southern New Hampshire. This rain fell over ground that was already wet from heavy rain the day before. Unofficial gage networks in the community of Rindge measured 3.80 inches. A washout occurred on School Street and other roads in town.
Heavy rainfall with rates over 3 inches and hour caused Youngs Brook to overflow its banks. The Brook flooded Browns Ridge Road at Youngs Road in Ossipee.

Showers with heavy rainfall rates formed over the White Mountains with rates up to 3 inches per hour. In Dixville Township, Golf Link Road washout cutting off access to private properties. Valley Road inaccessible due to flooding.
Showers with rainfall rates up to 3 inches and hour moved across Nelson on the 4th. Washouts were reported on Log Cabin Road and Old Stoddard Road.
Severe washouts on Center Pond Road flooded after torrential rain fell with rates up to 3 inches per hour.
Rain with torrential rainfall rates up to 3 inches per hour caused washouts on Barrett Pond Road.
Law enforcement reported basement flooding of Stoddard residents up to 3 feet deep.
Heavy rain caused multiple washouts on Pine Hill Road and Cape Moonshine Road in Haverhill.
Torrential rain caused washouts on Pine Hill Road and Cape Moonshine Road in Warren. Radar estimated rainfall rates up to 3 inches per hour.

Public reported a washout on Goodrich Road near Jackson Brook. Minor washout on Murray Street near McLaughlin Lane. Radar estimated 1 to 3 inches of rain fell across the Bingham Area in the course of an hour and a half.
Heavy rain on the afternoon of July 8th caused flooding on Tolman Pond and Bancroft Roads in Nelson. Some damage to the roads were reported, along with numerous private roads impacted.
Heavy rain on the evening of July 8th caused Western Avenue to close due to flooding near New England College.  Additional flooding was observed along Hall and Gould Street.

After multiple days of heavy rainfall, Swanzey Lake overflowed on July 9th. The flooding caused Swanzey Lake Road to washout and necessitated the evacuation of lakeshore residents.  Fire Department responded with the City of Keene (Cheshire County) swift water rescue team. This caused over 100 vehicles to become stranded and then required the evacuation of nearly 150 guests of the Pilgrim Pines Camp and Retreat Center.

Heavy rainfall measured around 4.5 inches caused the closure of main thruway Route 10 near Kapper Drive in Winchester on the afternoon of the 9th. An extensive washout on Route 10 required lengthy repairs to a 600 foot section of the road.

Severe widespread flooding in Swanzey prompted Police to issue a statement Please avoid driving in Swanzey at this time. Numerous roads across the community were flooded and damaged by floodwaters including Route 10, Holbrook Avenue, Old Homestead Highway, East Shore, and Carlton Roads, along with several others.
Heavy rain on the afternoon of the 9th caused several washouts along Graine Lake Road in Nelson. Murdough Hill Road also closed due to a washout.
Main thoroughfare NH-31 closed from Windsor town line to East Washington Road due to water over the roadway.
Heavy rain during the afternoon of the 9th caused overnight flooding of the Great Brook in Langdon. The Brook flooded Old Stage Road.
Several damaged and washed out roads in Enfield-Canaan area. South road was damaged between Potato Road and Grist Mill Road.

Heavy rain moved into Cheshire County around 8 PM with rainfall rates peaking around 4 inches an hour. In Walpole, Great Brook came out of banks and flooded Old Keene Road near Mill Road and damaged agricultural property off Watkins Hill Road.

Heavy rain moved into the Manchester area on the afternoon of the 15th. Urban runoff occurred after rainfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour fell. Numerous roads were closed due to flooding including Lake Avenue in the 500-block area with water entering a residence basement. Valley Street in the area of Belmont street was also closed due to flooding.

Heavy rainfall with rainfall rates between 2 and 4 inches per hours caused flooding and minor debris slide in Lincoln on the evening of the 15th. A debris flow was reported on Pinehill Lane and Charkarohen Drive closing the road and cutting off homes. Some minor property damage of yards.
Heavy rainfall with rates between 2 and 4 inches per hour fell over Antrim on the morning of the 16th. All lanes were closed on Washington Road from Center Road to Robbins Road due to flooding.

Bear Brook overflowed its banks after heavy rains moved into the state on the morning of the 16th. The brook was already running at bankfull prior to the storms arrival. The extra 1 to 3 inches of rain was sufficient to cause it to come out of banks and flood East Washington Road.
North Road in Danbury damaged after flooding caused part of the road collapsed near School Pond Road.
Heavy rain measured between 2 to 4 inches fell across the City of Manchester. Urban flooding was reported including the full closure of Commercial St in Manchester.
Heavy rain between 2 to 5 inches fell across the Madison area. Runoff caused the full road closure of Rt 113.
Heavy rain caused a washout on NH-109 in Wolfboro.

Heavy rain caused numerous road closures across Antrim. Whitney Road, Old Concord Road, Old Turnpike Road, Upper Pleasant Street. and more. On West St. On Buttercup Lane a culvert failed, and a section of roadway was damaged.
Flooding in South Hooksett prompted a full closure of NH-28A.

Heavy rain promoted renewed flooding in the Milford area after a period of frequent heavy rains across the state. By late morning of the 11th, flooding caused the closure of Route 101A in Milford from the Route 101 exit ramp to the downtown Milford area. One minor area of flowing water from a nearby swamp is crossing the road on Tonella Road.
Heavy rain caused a wash-out on White Oak Road.

Severe flooding reported across Alton after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell on the 16th. Ground conditions were saturated ahead of this event due to multiple heavy rain events the weeks prior to the flooding. The hardest hit areas were in central and southern Alton where several areas were impassable due to damaged roads. Flooding caused flooding of NH-140 near Gilmanton Fire Department. Numerous washouts were reported on Mount Major Highway. Jesus Valley Road was undermined due to an undersized culvert. ||The most devastating damages occurred on NH-140 near Elliot Road. A small brook coming out of Meadow Dam Pond flows southeast towards Elliot Road and Route 140. This brook produced significant flooding and undermined a hundred yard stretch of Route 140 and damaged several properties.
Heavy rain between 3 and 5 inches caused a large sinkhole on Cherry Valley Road, cutting off some residents.
Heavy rain between 3 and 5 inches caused multiple washouts on Will Smith Road, cutting off some residents.
Heavy rain between 3 and 5 inches caused a washout on Vail Road.
Heavy rain caused Route 28 in Wolfboro to wash-out between the Belknap and Carroll County line.
Heavy rain caused a washout on South Main Street in Wolfboro.
The main throughfare in Fryeburg, Route 302, flooded in the 300-block area causing significant disruption to travel in and out of the area.
Heavy rainfall between 3 and 5 inches caused a washout on Waterford Road in Norway.
Heavy rainfall between 3 and 5 inches caused a washout on High Street in South Paris around the 500-block area.
Heavy rainfall between 3 and 5 inches caused a washout on Waterford Road near the Crooked River.
Deep flood waters came off North Shore Road onto W Shore Road near the intersection with N Shore Road adjacent to Pleasant Pond.  The debris was over a foot deep.
Heavy rain estimated between 2 and 3 inches resulted in 1 foot of water flowing over Old County Road in West Paris.
Heavy rain estimated between 2 and 3 inches resulted in washouts on Curtis Hill Road, Andrews Road, Perkins Valley Road, and Cushman Road.
Heavy rain over saturated ground resulted in washouts on Martins Brook Road in Wentworth. Shoulder washouts also occurred on Clifford Brook Road.
Zealand River came out of banks resulting in evacuations at an adjacent campground after Zealand Road flooded.
Heavy rain caused the Tuttle Brook to come out of banks and cause some minor damage to the Recreational Area off Lake Road.
Severe washouts on Perry Road and Mountain Road in multiple locations near Dead Pond cutting off properties.
Heavy rain caused a washout on Cates Hill Road.
Heavy rain caused a washout on Corser Brook Road in Errol.

Torrential showers brought rainfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour to the southern portions of Nashua on the afternoon of the 21st. The public reported 2 feet of water over Daniel Webster Highway and flooding into homes and apartments.
Tucker Valley Brook in Wilton overflowed onto Rollins Ridge Road resulting in a significant washout estimated at 12 yards long and up to 2 lanes wide.

Heavy rain reported at 3 to 5 inches fell across the Lewiston/Auburn area during the early evening hours of the 25th. This nearly stationary storm caused major disruptions to the evening commute as a number of primary thruways were closed. The flooding started in Lewiston when North Temple Road closed, followed shortly by Main Street. Cars stalled and were submerged in the floodwaters. As the event unfolded the flooding extended to southern Lewiston over Adams Avenue near the Public Works Department, and flooded parking lots at Bates College.

Heavy rain reported at 3 to 5 inches fell across the Lewiston/Auburn area during the early evening hours of the 25th. This nearly stationary storm caused major disruptions to the evening commute as a number of primary thruways were closed. The worst hit areas were Court Street near the river, Center Street, and Route 202.
Heavy rain caused a washout on Howe Lane near Newmarket Road in Warner.
Back Brook overflowed onto Whaleback Road in Limington following heavy rainfall estimated between 2 to 3 inches.
Portion of Route 237 closed between Chadborne Road and Barstow Road due to flooding. Water deep enough to float a car.
Heavy rainfall estimated between 2 and 3 inches with high rainfall rates caused a washout on the side of Dube drive in Lisbon.
Heavy rainfall with rates between 2 and 4 inches per hour caused a significant washout on Doughty Road.
Heavy rain caused a washout on Burt Hill Road  due to rushing water off steep terrain off Gun Mountain.
Heavy rain caused a washout on Avery Hill Road due to rushing water off steep terrain.

Flooding caused by the significant rainfall over two days damaged property and roads in the Marlow area.  Most roads were closed due to flooding and residents were advised to stay home.  The flooding produced on the 10-11th of July occurred over areas that were already dealing with previous flooding. The North Fork of the already flooded Ashuelot River flooded portions of Marlow. Another source of flooding came when the Stoddard Lake overflowed totally surounding homes.

Multiple rounds of heavy rain caused a washout on Currier Road in Langdon on the afternoon of the 10th. Rainfall that afternoon was estimated between 1 to 2 inches, however saturated ground and recent heavy rain contributed to the severity of the flooding.
Hill Road flooded from Darby Brook near Drewsville Road.

The Suncook River came out of  banks following heavy rain on the 2nd. The water came up to Bachelder Road in Allenstown. Waterfront campsites upstream were inundated. The river crested at 7.5 feet, flood stage is 7.0 feet.

Heavy rains on July 16th lead to flooding along the Suncook River. The USGS river gage in North Chichester crested at 10.5 feet on the 17th. The flood stage is 7 feet, and the river crested at the minor flood level. The impacts were most notable at the Lazy River Campground where water inundated campsites with 2 to 3 feet of water. Numerous campers had to be evacuated. Water came out of banks in Allenstown, but did not, but did not cause any property damage.

The Sugar River overflowed its banks between the 10th-11th. The flood stage for the USGS river gage at Claremont has a flood stage of 7.0 feet, and on the 11th the river crested at 8.49 feet. A campground in Newport was inundated by floodwaters. Corbin Road from NH10 to the covered bridge flooded.

The Connecticut River at West Lebanon flooded between July 10-11. The USGS river gage at West Lebanon has a flood stage of 22 feet and crested at 22.9 feet on the 11th.  The river was out of banks and caused minor inundation of a showing plaza parking lot and property adjacent to the publics water department in Lebanon.

The Connecticut River at Walpole flooded on July 11. The USGS river gage at West Walpole has a flood stage of 28 feet and crested at 28.2 feet on the 11th.  The river was out of banks and caused minor inundation along the river from Walpole and Westminster downstream to the Massachusetts border. Portions of low-lying agricultural lands adjacent to river were inundated. The most impactful flooding was in Brattleboro, however that was primarily caused by flooding from the Whetstone Brook which is a tributary to the Connecticut River.

The Saco River came out of banks on July 11th following heavy rain showers. The USGS river gage at Conway exceeded the flood stage of 9 feet, cresting at 9.4 feet on the 11th. The impacts were mainly focused at low lying campgrounds and flooding at Transvale Road.

The Contoocook River exceeded flood stage on the 11th following multiple rounds of heavy rain across the watershed. The USGS river gage at Henniker exceeded flood stage of 12.0 feet cresting at 12.36 feet. Impacts were considered minor with floodwaters up to Henniker Street and Bear Hill Road in Hillsborough.

The Saco River came out of banks on July 16th following heavy rain showers. The USGS river gage at Conway exceeded the flood stage of 9 feet, cresting at 8.3 feet on the 16th. The impacts were mainly focused at low lying campgrounds and flooding at Transvale Road.

The Swift River came out of banks on July 16th following heavy rain showers. The USGS river gage at Roxbury exceeded the flood stage of 7 feet, cresting at 9.2 feet on the 16th. The impacts were flooding of Route 17 in Byron.

Island Pond in Cheshire County reached significant levels following multiple rounds of heavy rainfall. Properties along the lake in Stoddard were flooded. On the evening of the 10th officials released water at the Island Pond Dam in Stoddard, which caused the water in the North Branch to overtop the Liberty Farm Road bridge in Antrim through the 11th. This cut off access to 18 homes.

The Cold River came out of banks on the evening of the 10th following heavy rains. The river had been running high due to multiple rounds of heavy rain over the previous few days. After approximately 1 to 3 inches of additional rain that afternoon, the river spiked to the second highest level on record at the Alstead USGS river gage (period of record 2010-2023). The river crested at 11.67 feet, with a discharge of 10,300 cfs. The flow recorded has an annual exceedance probability between 1% and 0.2% levels.  The high flowing water came out of banks along Route-123A in South Acworth and Acworth Road in Alstead. Acworth Fire Chief rescued 12 people from their homes on Route 123A. He said several cars were swept by water but there were no injuries in those incidents. The floodwaters caused damage to the southbound lane on Acworth Road. In Lempster South Road and River Road were flooded.

Following several days of heavy rainfall caused a breach in the Forest Lake Road dam. The initial breach caused flooding on Route 10, and then flowed into the Ashuelot River where the flood wave dampened.

The Ashuelot River flooded Gilsum Road between Gilsum and Surry. The USGS river gage at Gilsum crested at 11.36 feet. The gage has a period of record of 100 years, and this event's crest was the 5th highest. No official flood stages are known, but the rarity of the discharge of 7,410 cfs is reported to have an annual exceedance probability of 0.2% a year.
Heavy rain caused the Partridge Brook to flood and washout a portion of Partridge Brook Road in Westmoreland.
Jefferson Road flooded with one lane closed due to heavy rain on the afternoon of the 10th.
Heavy rain over saturated ground caused a washout to the southbound lane of US-3 at mile 227.4 in Pittsburg.
Heavy rain over saturated ground led to flooding on Pinneo Hill Road near Lyme Road in Hanover.
The Smith River came out of banks and flooded Bohannon Road, Eastern District Road, North Road, Sheep Rock Road, and Spa Road. The floodwaters were slow to rise and slow to recede.

The Blackwater River came out of banks and flooded portions of Route 4 in Andover between Plains Road and NH-11. The flooding was the result of multiple rounds of heavy rainfall over a 7 day period, tipped over into flooding by 1 to 3 inches of rainfall on the 10th. The river was slow to rise and slower to recede.
Flooding on Long Pond and Lempster Mountain Road in Lempster caused by overflow of the headwaters of the Ashuelot River.

Lake Sunapee reached a record highest level for the time of year in July.  Water releases from the lake into the Sugar River caused flooding on Brook Road between Natures Way and NH RT 103. Other roads flooded include Reeds Mill Road from Old Springfield Road to NH103.
Lake Sunapee reached a record level for summer resulting in floodings of lakeshore properties. Outbuildings and docks were impacted by floodwaters.
Overflow from Gilman Pond combined with local runoff caused the Spring Brook to come out of banks. The Brook flooded Unity Springs Road where a water rescue was conducted.

Heavy rainfall measured between 3 and 5 inches fell across southwest Androscoggin County on the 8th. The runoff caused significant flooding to a number of roads across Auburn, Poland, and Minot. West Auburn Road near Summer Street was flooded to a depth that cut off emergency access. Park Avenue, Lakeshore Drive, Broad Street between Witham and Hackett Roads, and Jackson Hill Roads also flooded and were closed due to flooding. In Poland, Bailey Hill Road flooded. Numerous basements were flooded in the Auburn area with water several feet deep.

Washout on Deer Run Road near Collins Road, caused by runoff from nearby hills and Jock Stream.

Heavy rain between 2 and 5 inches fell across the Gray/New Gloucester area on August 8th. The heavy rain was spread out over 6 hours, with rates up to 2 inches an hour. The excessive runoff caused flooding on a number of roads. Legrow Road, Lewiston Road, and most notably Route 202 causing significant disruptions to travel in and out of the community.

Heavy rainfall between 2 to 4 inches fell over the Royal River watershed on the 8th. The river responded by coming out of banks during the afternoon into the overnight hours. In New Gloucester, Route 231 flooded between Woodman Road and Cobbs Bridge Road. Upstream the river flooded low lying  sections of Meadow Lane near Cobbs Bridge road.
Route 100 near Deer Run Drive in Cumberland flooded by the Piscataqua River.

Heavy rain between 3 and 5 inches caused a sinkhole along Babbidge Road near Spoondrift Road. The sinkhole damaged the shoulder and part of one lane. The road continued to collapse into the afternoon resulting in a full closure, but the flooding that undermined the road occurred during the morning hours.
Sebago Lake Road or Route 237 between Standish and Gorham flooded. The flooding occurred in a low spot between Route 35 and Barstow Road near a boggy area that overflowed.

State officials reported nearly one mile of Route 17 between Byron and Rangeley Plantation in Franklin County was damaged by flash flooding. Route 4 was also washed out and closed near Sandy River Plantation around the same time.
Water from Mill Stream came over Embden Pond Road in Embden. Flooding also occurred on nearby Slipp and Fahi Pond Road.
Heavy rain on the 8th caused washouts on Davis and Mason Roads in Vienna near Eaton Mountain, resulting in the closure of Davis Road and 2 spots on Mason Road.
Shoulder washout on Hovey Road near US RT 2 in Farmington with water surrounding a home and flooding an outbuilding.

Multiple areas in downtown Plaistow including Town Green, Main Street, and Congressional Avenue were flooded with flowing water across streets and feet of standing water up to knee depth in parts. South of town the main thruway Route 108 or Newton Road was closed due to flooding.
Shoulder damage washout on local Morrill Road in Norway caused by heavy rain with rates up to 2 inches per hour. Total rainfall was around 2 and a half inches as estimated by radar.

An un-named tributary to the Sugar River flows from south to north out of Hubbard Hill came out of banks on the 8th. Floodwaters damaged the intersection of Roberts Road and Borough Road. An unofficial weather station in the community measured over 2 and a half inches, with instantaneous rain rates peaking over 4 inches an hour around 5 PM. Radar estimated a storm total rainfall between 2.5 to 3.5 inches over the Charlestown area.

Unofficial rain gage stations reported rainfall amounts between 2 to 6 inches between Hollis, Nashua, and Hudson. Nashua Fire Department responded to multiple calls of people trapped in their cars. There were about a dozen reports of flooded basements, according to Nashua Emergency Management. Both Dow Road and Twiss Lane remained closed for a long duration due to damage from floodwaters. A parking area to an apartment complex off Northeastern Boulevard had up to 4 feet of standing water, damaging dozens of cars.
NH-130, also known as Proctor Road, was closed due to flood waters between Rocky Pond Rd and Kerk Drive. Floods damaged Proctor Hill Road from Rocky Pond Rd in Hollis to the Brookline town line.

Water several feet deep in June street with reports upwards of 3-4FT. Flooding was caused by heavy rainfall on the evening of the 11th. Unofficial weather station in the Hudson area recorded over 5 inches of rain between 5 and 8 PM.

No inundation flooding was reported, but there was high surf on the Saturday midday high tide cycle as long period 10 to 11 foot swells reached the coast. As Post-Tropical Lee traveled east of the coastal waters, strong northerly offshore winds impacted the coastal waters.  The Penobscot Bay Buoy had a sustained wind of 37kts with a peak gust of 49kts.  Two wave sets from the offshore locally generate waves battled the long period swell set from the southeast direction.  This led to choppy waters and a peak wave height of 7.7ft.

Precipitation began around midday on the 3rd as a wintry mix of rain and snow. Downsloping easterly flow, which was both warmer and drier than on the upslope side of the White Mountains, kept precipitation type mainly rain or very light snow. The east facing slopes stayed predominately snow. This led to a large range in snowfall totals from the higher terrain in the eastern parts of the North Country to the west near the Connecticut River. Eventually steady snow tapered to upslope snow showers, which continued for most of the day on the 4th. Snowfall totals ranged from 10 inches near the Maine border to 5 inches near First Connecticut Lake.

Strong southeast wind gusts began the morning of the 18th. While wind gusts remained strong throughout the day, the damaging gusts occurred in several waves during the morning, again at midday, and once more in the evening. The peak gusts were fairly typical of a high wind event during the cool season, but the duration of the strong to damaging winds was much longer than usual. So while 50 to 60 mph wind gusts did some damage alone, the persistent gusts brought down limbs and trees and damaged powerlines. Around 30 percent of electrical customers were without power by the evening of the 18th.

The peak gusts were fairly typical of a high wind event during the cool season, but the duration of the strong to damaging winds was much longer than usual. So while 50 to 60 mph wind gusts did some damage alone, the persistent gusts brought down limbs and trees and damaged powerlines. Around 40 percent of electrical customers were without power by the evening of the 18th.  A man died when a tree fell on him when he was removing tree debris from his yard.

Winds quickly diminished once the frontal occlusion moved through the North Country.

Significant flooding occurred from Woodstock to Plymouth after a storm brought 3 to 6 inches of combined rain and snow melt to the region.  The heaviest rainfall and most significant snowmelt water contribution occurred across the higher terrain of the watershed, where up to 10 inches of combined rainfall and snowmelt was released into the Pemigewasset basin.  This caused the river to rise to its third highest crest at Woodstock, and 10th highest on record at Plymouth. This was also the highest crest on the Pemigewasset since Tropical Storm Irene in 2011. Estimates near the start of the watershed put the flow in the 1.0 to 0.5% chance of exceedance levels, also referred to as a 100-200 year flood event. It was less significant downstream however, with estimated flows at Woodstock being more consistent with a 25-50 year, and flows at Plymouth being more consistent with a 25 year event. The decreasing recurrence interval timeframe with downstream progress on the river highlights the significant role the higher rainfall amounts and snowmelt factored in near the top of the watershed, while relatively less input with decreasing elevation resulted in a tapering in the relative significance of the event. Damage was widespread along the Pemigewasset between Woodstock to Ashland.  In the town of Holderness, up to two feet of water entered homes and local businesses on Avery Street, South River St, and North River St.  Individuals that declined to evacuate were stuck in their homes as floodwaters entered during the early morning hours on the 19th.  Water levels rose to the edge of the Plymouth State University Ice Arena doors.  Numerous road closures were reported along Route 3, with up to five feet of water covering the roadways in Plymouth and Campton.  Water up to two feet deep covered Route 3 in Thornton, and flooded numerous trailers and campers at local riverside campgrounds.  Anecdotally, locals reported that the water levels in Thornton were higher than they were during Irene.

The Ammonoosuc River reached moderate flood stage on December 18th. The USGS river gage in Bethlehem reported a stage of 12.15 feet, the second highest crest on record since the site was established in 1940. The flooding was the result of heavy rainfall combined with snowmelt in the mountains. The combined runoff was estimated between 6 and 7 inches which moved rapidly down steep terrain over frozen ground. The river rose from 2 feet to over 12 feet within 15 hours, cresting in the early afternoon of the 18th. In upstream Bethlehem, there was flooding along several small streams and brooks.  Access was cut off on River Road with flooding in multiple locations.  Significant flooding occurred upstream at Twin Mountain and Zealand Campgrounds. Flooding occurred at the Stark Village Inn with basement inundation and water up to the bottom of the covered bridge in Stark.
